content: 1. Patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) have been the focus of numerous studies, including those accessible through the National Institutes of Health (NIH) clinical trials database. The WHO has issued consolidated guidelines on the treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis, emphasizing best practices for the off-label use of bedaquiline and delamanid in MDR-TB management. 2. Tang et al. conducted a study in China evaluating the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of linezolid for the treatment of extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB). The findings, published in the European Respiratory Journal in 2015, demonstrated promising outcomes. 3. Thwaites et al. performed a randomized pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic comparison of fluoroquinolones for the treatment of tuberculous meningitis. Their research, published in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy in 2011, provided critical insights into optimizing treatment regimens. 4. Donald PR reviewed the chemotherapy of tuberculous meningitis in both children and adults, highlighting the challenges and therapeutic strategies. This comprehensive review was published in the journal Tuberculosis in 2010. 5. Sun et al. reported that linezolid exhibits a rapid and dramatic therapeutic effect in patients with life-threatening tuberculous meningitis. Their findings, published in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy in 2014, underscore the potential of linezolid in critical cases. 6. The WHO, in collaboration with the Global Fund and the Global Drug Facility (GDF), released a document addressing frequently asked questions about the WHO Rapid Communication on key changes to the treatment of MDR-TB and rifampicin-resistant TB. 7. A technical report on the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) of medicines used in the treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis was published, providing a detailed analysis of drug behavior and efficacy. 8. The use of next-generation sequencing technologies for detecting mutations associated with drug resistance in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex has been explored in a technical guide, emphasizing its role in advancing diagnostic capabilities. 9. Guidelines for the surveillance of drug resistance in tuberculosis, now in their fifth edition, provide a framework for monitoring and addressing resistance patterns globally. 10. The FDA briefing package for Sirturo™ (bedaquiline) outlines its use as part of combination therapy for pulmonary MDR-TB in adults aged 18 years and older. This document was presented during the FDA Anti-Infective Drugs Advisory Committee Meeting in 2012. 11. The European Medicines Agency (EMA) provides detailed information on the use of Sirturo (bedaquiline) and Deltyba (delamanid) for the treatment of MDR-TB, accessible through their respective online platforms. 12. The WHO has emphasized the importance of electronic recording and reporting systems for tuberculosis care and control, highlighting their role in improving treatment outcomes and program efficiency. 13. Nunn et al. described the STREAM trial protocol, which evaluates a standardized treatment regimen for MDR-TB through a randomized controlled trial. The study aims to optimize treatment strategies for MDR-TB patients. 14. The WHO issued a position statement on the continued use of shorter MDR-TB regimens following an expedited review of preliminary results from the STREAM Stage 1 trial. 15. Van Deun et al. demonstrated the effectiveness of a short, standardized, and cost-effective treatment regimen for MDR-TB in a study published in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine in 2010. 16. Kuaban et al. reported high effectiveness of a 12-month MDR-TB treatment regimen in Cameroon, as published in the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease in 2015. 17. Piubello et al. documented high cure rates with standardized short-course MDR-TB treatment in Niger, with no relapses observed. This study was published in 2014. 18. Trebucq et al. evaluated treatment outcomes with a short MDR-TB regimen across nine African countries, highlighting its success in the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease in 2018. 19. The WHO released a position statement on the use of shorter MDR-TB regimens, emphasizing their potential to improve treatment outcomes and accessibility. 20. Kurbatova et al. analyzed the frequency and type of microbiological monitoring during MDR-TB treatment, providing valuable insights into optimizing patient management. 21. Mitnick et al. highlighted the importance of monitoring intervals and microbiological methods in detecting MDR-TB treatment failure, as published in the European Respiratory Journal in 2016. 22. The WHO Tuberculosis Laboratory Biosafety Manual provides comprehensive guidelines for ensuring safety in TB diagnostic and research laboratories. 23. Friedrich et al. assessed the sensitivity and specificity of the Xpert MTB/RIF assay as an early sputum biomarker for TB treatment response, with findings published in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine in 2013. 24. Jayakumar et al. demonstrated that the Xpert MTB/RIF assay shows faster clearance of Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA with higher rifapentine exposure levels, as reported in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology in 2016. 25. Burgos et al. described an outpatient-based approach to MDR-TB treatment in San Francisco, highlighting its effectiveness in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2005. 26. Dheda et al. examined early treatment outcomes and HIV status in patients with XDR-TB in South Africa, publishing their findings in The Lancet in 2010. 27. Eker et al. reported on MDRand XDR-TB cases in Germany, emphasizing the challenges and outcomes in managing these cases, as published in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2008. 28. El Sahly et al. analyzed drug-resistant TB as a disease of target populations in Houston, Texas, with findings published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2006. 29. Leimane et al. reviewed treatment outcomes for MDR/XDR-TB in Latvia from 2000 to 2004, as published in the European Respiratory Journal in 2010. 30. Migliori et al. discussed the clinical and operational value of the XDR-TB definition, providing insights into its implications for treatment and management. 31. Palmero et al. examined MDR-TB in AIDS patients at the beginning of the millennium, with findings published in Medicina (Mexico) in 2006. 32. The WHO consolidated guidelines on drug-resistant TB treatment provide a comprehensive framework for managing these challenging cases. 33. Shean et al. reviewed treatment outcomes and follow-up of MDR-TB patients in South Africa, highlighting the importance of long-term monitoring. 34. Varma et al. identified factors associated with improved survival during TB treatment in HIV-positive patients in Thailand, as published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2009. 35. Jamal et al. evaluated the reliability and usefulness of TB/HIV co-infection data from developing countries, presenting their findings at the XV International AIDS Conference in 2004. 36. Abdool Karim et al. investigated the timing of antiretroviral therapy initiation during TB treatment, with findings published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2010. 37. Blanc et al. demonstrated significant survival benefits with early initiation of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) in severely immunosuppressed HIV-infected adults with TB. 38. Fox et al. conducted a meta-analysis on the role of surgery as an adjunctive treatment for MDR-TB, highlighting its potential benefits in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2016. 39. Harris et al. systematically reviewed the impact of surgery on MDR-TB treatment outcomes, publishing their findings in BMC Infectious Diseases. 40. Bayer and Wilkinson reviewed the history and implementation of directly observed therapy (DOT) for TB, emphasizing its role in improving treatment adherence and outcomes. 41. Kamolratanakul et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial of DOT for pulmonary TB patients in Thailand, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving treatment outcomes. 42. MacIntyre et al. evaluated the efficacy of family-based direct observation of anti-TB treatment in an urban, developed-country setting, as published in the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease. 43. The Tuberculosis Research Centre conducted a controlled clinical trial of oral short-course regimens for sputum-positive pulmonary TB, providing evidence for their effectiveness. 44. Walley et al. assessed the effectiveness of the direct observation component of DOTS in Pakistan, publishing their findings in The Lancet in 2001. 45. Zwarenstein et al. compared self-supervised and directly observed treatment of TB in a randomized controlled trial, highlighting the importance of supervision in improving outcomes. 46. Zwarenstein et al. also evaluated the role of lay health workers as direct observers for TB treatment, demonstrating their effectiveness in the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease. 47. Tandon et al. compared DOTS with self-administered therapy for pulmonary TB patients in a randomized trial at a tertiary care hospital in India, highlighting the benefits of DOTS. 48. Akkslip et al. evaluated the use of supervised family members for direct observation of TB treatment in Thailand, demonstrating its feasibility and effectiveness. 49. Balasubramanian et al. examined the impact of direct observation on anti-TB treatment outcomes in Kerala State, India, providing evidence for its benefits. 50. Mathema et al. conducted a rapid assessment of TB treatment in Nepal, comparing different types of patient supervision in government centers. 51. Ormerod et al. reviewed TB treatment outcome monitoring in Blackburn from 1988 to 2000, providing insights into long-term trends and challenges. 52. Tsuchida and Koyanagi evaluated the outcomes of DOT for TB in Yokohama City, Japan, highlighting its role in improving treatment adherence and success rates. 53. Nirupa et al. assessed the performance of directly observed treatment providers in the Revised National Tuberculosis Control Programme in India, emphasizing their importance in achieving treatment success. 54. Daniel OJ reviewed the preand post-DOT era in TB management at a teaching hospital, highlighting the improvements achieved with DOT implementation. 55. Okanurak et al. conducted a prospective cohort study on the effectiveness of DOT for TB treatment outcomes in Bangkok, Thailand, demonstrating its benefits. 56. Abassi and Mansourian evaluated the efficacy of the DOTS strategy in treating respiratory TB in Gorgan, Iran, providing evidence for its success. 57. Siemion-Szczesniak and Kus reviewed treatment outcomes in culture-positive pulmonary TB, emphasizing the importance of adherence to treatment protocols. 58. Caylà et al. analyzed TB treatment adherence and fatality rates in Spain, providing insights into factors influencing treatment success. 59. Zvavamwe and Ehlers reviewed the experiences of a community-based TB treatment program in Namibia, highlighting its effectiveness in improving outcomes. 60. Xu et al. conducted a mixed-methods study on adherence to anti-TB treatment among pulmonary TB patients, providing valuable insights into barriers and facilitators. 61. Abuaku et al. examined treatment default and death among TB patients in Hunan, China, identifying factors associated with poor outcomes. 62. Ershova et al. evaluated adherence to national treatment guidelines among TB patients in South Africa, emphasizing the importance of guideline-based care. 63. Weis et al. demonstrated that DOT reduces rates of drug resistance and relapse in TB, as published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1994. 64. Bashar et al. reported an increased incidence of MDR-TB in diabetic patients at Bellevue Chest Service, highlighting the need for targeted interventions. 65. Olle-Goig and Alvarez reviewed TB treatment in rural Haiti, comparing directly observed and non-observed regimens, and emphasizing the benefits of DOT. 66. Pungprassami et al. evaluated the impact of DOT on TB treatment outcomes in southern Thailand, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving adherence and success rates. 67. Jasmer et al. compared DOT with self-administered therapy for TB treatment, highlighting the advantages of DOT in achieving better outcomes. 68. Cavalcante et al. compared community-based DOT with clinic-based models in a Brazilian favela, demonstrating the feasibility and success of community-based approaches. 69. Radilla-Chávez and Laniado-Laborín reviewed the results of DOT for TB treatment, emphasizing its role in improving adherence and outcomes.
